Article Title: Anthropic launches Claude Fable 5.2, Mythos 5.2 with faster performance and stronger coding capabilities
Article Text:
Faster responses and lower pricing

Benchmark improvements

Cybersecurity

Safety

Availability

Anthropic has announced its latest frontier AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, saying the new systems deliver significant improvements in coding, reasoning, visual understanding and scientific problem-solving while also running faster and at a lower cost than their predecessors. According to Anthropic, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are designed to tackle highly complex technical tasks. During pre-release testing, the company said the models helped engineers complete software migrations, design electronic devices from scratch, make progress on robotics evaluations and assist with advanced mathematical and scientific problems.Anthropic said Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are based on the same underlying model. However, Fable includes enhanced cybersecurity and biology safeguards that allow it to be broadly available, while access to Mythos is restricted to organisations pursuing approved cybersecurity and biomedical research applications through the company's verification programmes.The company said the new models generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1. Anthropic has priced the models at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, while an optional fast mode offering up to 2.5-times faster token generation is available at higher pricing tiers.Anthropic claims the latest models outperform its own Claude Opus 5.5 across a wide range of benchmarks covering agentic coding, scientific research, business workflows, cybersecurity, robotics, visual chart recognition and multidisciplinary reasoning. On the FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark, Fable 5.2 achieved a score of 49.1%, which the company described as the highest score among released models it has tested.The company also highlighted efficiency gains, noting that Fable 5.2 can complete challenging tasks using fewer tokens than Fable 5.1 and, in some benchmarks, delivers performance comparable to Opus 5.5 at roughly half the cost per task.Anthropic calls Mythos 5.2 its most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. On its internal CVE Rediscovery test, it found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Mythos 5.1. Mozilla said it roughly doubled vulnerability-discovery metrics compared with Mythos 5.1. Fable 5.2’s classifiers block most high-risk cyber tasks and most research biology tasks. Anthropic said blocks are about 55% fewer than with Fable 5.1.Anthropic said it judges the risk of the models behaving unsafely in high-stakes situations to be low, and that testing by the UK AI Security Institute, Frontier Design and METR preceded release. It also said the models voice suspicion that they’re being evaluated more often than recent models, which complicates how well tests predict real-world behaviour. The company said Fable 5.2 has its strongest protections yet against illicit distillation, cutting data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%. It also said it limited advances in research capabilities that could most directly speed up AI development.Fable 5.2 is available now on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure, and for developers as claude-fable-5-2. Cybersecurity professionals can apply for Mythos 5.2 through the Cyber Verification Program, and life sciences researchers through a separate program. Enterprise customers can also reach Mythos 5.2 through Claude Security. Eligible paid subscribers are getting extra Fable usage this week as a launch promotion.
Article Summary: Claude Fable and Claude Mythos 5.2 are based on the same underlying model. Fable includes enhanced cybersecurity and biology safeguards that allow it to be broadly available. Access to Mythos is restricted to organisations pursuing approved cybersecurity and biomedical research applications.

Article Title: Experts in Canada are testing doorbell cameras' for Polar bears, called Bear-vision, they combine radar and cameras to …
Article Text:
Image Credit: Alan Wilson/Wikipedia

How will Bear-vision work

Why is Churchill’s waste facility the first location

Why are bears spending longer near communities

What other tools are researchers testing

“It’s not easy to live with large predators as your neighbours, so we’re investing in coexistence approaches, especially as we see climate change causing more human-bear encounters. By developing and field-testing innovative, non-lethal deterrents like drones and detection tech like Bear-vision, we’re hoping to expand the variety of safe, effective, and affordable coexistence tools available to communities,”

Researchers are testing Bear-vision cameras to warn communities in Canada about approaching polar bears. Conservation charity Polar Bears International is developing Bear-vision, a warning system built on security camera technology that can be paired with shorter-range radar. Its first deployment is planned at Churchill’s waste facility this autumn to help monitor bears and reduce surprise encounters, the organisation’ noted in a blog post.The camera is intended to offer a more affordable, easy-to-use alternative to wide-area radar systems. Researchers will use data gathered at the site to train it to recognise polar bears and send notifications when they appear. The project comes as bears gather along Hudson Bay, waiting for sea ice to return so they can hunt seals, while communities work to keep people and wildlife safely apart.Bear-vision builds on the organisation’s earlier Bear-dar detection work. While Bear-dar monitors wider areas using radar, the new system uses smart security camera technology and can incorporate shorter-range radar.​Polar Bears International compares the intended function to a doorbell camera that alerts residents when a polar bear is outside. The Churchill deployment will help researchers gather the information needed to train the notification system.Churchill began working with Polar Bears International to keep bears out of its dump after a fire destroyed its waste facilities. Garbage can attract bears looking for food, creating risks for both the animals and people nearby.The response includes new electric fences, Bear-dar and Bear-vision monitoring, and a visit by a Churchill delegation to a waste management facility in Greenland. The camera trial is part of a broader effort to manage the site, not replace physical barriers or other measures.Polar Bears International says climate-driven sea ice loss leaves bears waiting on land about a month longer than their grandparents did. The ice-free period around Hudson Bay now lasts three to four weeks longer than in the 1980s, placing additional strain on their stored fat reserves.The organisation says these longer periods ashore make coexistence measures increasingly important. Its Polar Bear Week, running November 1–7, coincides with the seasonal gathering near Churchill.Polar Bears International and Brigham Young University are also working with Churchill’s Polar Bear Alert Program to test drones as an affordable, non-lethal way to move bears away from communities. That separate deterrent project includes ultrasonic sound, conductive materials and a new odour-based bear spray formula.said Geoff York, Polar Bears International’s vice president of science and policy.
Article Summary: Polar Bears International is developing Bear-vision, a warning system built on security camera technology that can be paired with shorter-range radar. Its first deployment is planned at Churchill’s waste facility this autumn. Researchers will use data gathered at the site to train it to recognise polar bears and send notifications when they appear.

Article Title: India’s Aditya-L1 unlocks Sun's secrets: How new discovery could help predict solar storms that threaten Earth
Article Text:
The Sun is not a completely stable ball of hot gas. Its magnetic field is constantly changing, creating conditions that can trigger powerful eruptions from its outer atmosphere.

What are solar eruptions and why do they matter?

What are coronal mass ejections?

Why are solar storms difficult to predict?

How Aditya-L1 observed the solar eruption

How Aditya-L1 uncovered the hidden dimension

Two observations combined.

Why does the shape of a solar eruption matter?

Can satellites protect themselves from solar storms?

Could Aditya-L1 help improve solar-storm forecasts?

About Aditya-L1

The Sun may be millions of kilometres away, but powerful eruptions on its surface can have consequences for life on Earth. From satellite-based navigation and communication to electricity networks, several technologies people depend on can be affected when these eruptions send enormous amounts of charged particles towards our planet.India's Aditya-L1 solar mission has helped scientists uncover a previously hidden aspect of how these eruptions behave. The discovery could help researchers better understand how solar storms travel through space and, eventually, improve predictions of when they might reach Earth.Scientists from the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), Bengaluru, found that a solar eruption observed in August 2024 did not expand uniformly like a symmetrical bubble. Instead, it expanded unevenly, developing an asymmetric shape.The finding, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, challenges a commonly used assumption about how these eruptions expand close to the Sun. Researchers arrived at the conclusion by combining observations from Aditya-L1's Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC), images from Nasa 's Solar Dynamics Observatory and three-dimensional modelling.But why does the shape of an eruption matter? And how could understanding its movement help scientists predict solar storms that can disrupt satellites, navigation systems and power infrastructure?The Sun is not a completely stable ball of hot gas. Its magnetic field is constantly changing, creating conditions that can trigger powerful eruptions from its outer atmosphere.One such phenomenon is a coronal mass ejection (CME). It involves the release of enormous quantities of hot, magnetised plasma from the Sun's outermost atmospheric layer, known as the corona. These eruptions can travel through interplanetary space at high speeds, carrying magnetic fields and charged particles with them.When a CME is directed towards Earth, it can interact with the planet's magnetic field and trigger a geomagnetic storm. The strength of the disturbance depends on several factors, including the speed and magnetic properties of the incoming eruption.Such storms are not merely astronomical events. They can affect technologies that modern societies increasingly depend on, particularly those operating in space or relying on satellite-based systems.Satellites can experience disruptions to their operations and, in severe cases, damage to onboard electronics. Solar activity can also affect radio communications and interfere with the accuracy of satellite-based navigation systems such as GPS. Strong geomagnetic disturbances can induce electrical currents in power transmission networks, potentially putting transformers and other grid equipment under stress.The effects can extend to aviation, particularly high-frequency radio communications and operations on polar routes, where exposure to space-weather disturbances can be greater.Chethan Kumar, a space expert and journalist who has extensively covered the extraterrestrial field, said solar storms can affect several systems simultaneously, including electricity supplies, radio signals and satellite-based applications.“Solar storms are also known to interfere with positioning services, so your GPS can get affected. When GPS gets affected, your air travel becomes less reliable, and it's a cascading effect,” he said.This makes the ability to monitor and forecast solar activity important for satellite operators, communication networks, aviation authorities and power-grid managers.However, predicting the behaviour of a CME after it leaves the Sun remains a complex scientific challenge. Scientists need to establish not only where an eruption is heading but also how fast it is moving and how its structure changes as it travels through space.One of the biggest challenges in studying CMEs is understanding their movement in three dimensions, particularly during the initial stages of an eruption.Scientists use instruments called coronagraphs to observe CMEs. These instruments block the bright solar disc, allowing researchers to study the much fainter corona and track eruptions as they move away from the Sun.However, conventional coronagraph images primarily capture movement across the observer's field of view. In other words, they show how an eruption travels across the sky but cannot directly establish how fast the plasma is moving towards or away from the observer.This missing information is important because a CME is a three-dimensional structure, not a flat object moving across an image.Two eruptions that appear similar in conventional images could have different three-dimensional shapes and expansion patterns. Their interactions with the surrounding solar wind could therefore differ, potentially affecting how their speeds change during propagation.Scientists have traditionally relied on observations from multiple spacecraft positioned at different locations to reconstruct the three-dimensional evolution of CMEs. While this provides valuable information, studying eruptions close to the Sun remains particularly challenging because they evolve rapidly during these early stages.This is where Aditya-L1's VELC instrument offers an additional observational capability.VELC is one of the primary scientific instruments onboard Aditya-L1. It was developed by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics in Bengaluru, with substantial support from Isro Unlike instruments that only capture images, VELC also records spectra, allowing scientists to study changes in the wavelength of light emitted by the solar corona.The technique is known as Doppler spectroscopy. It is based on the principle that the wavelength of light changes depending on the movement of the source relative to the observer.For instance, when plasma moves towards an observer, the light it emits shifts towards shorter wavelengths, known as a blue shift. When it moves away, the wavelength shifts towards the longer, red end of the spectrum.This allows scientists to measure movement along the line of sight, the direction between the observed object and the observer, which conventional images cannot directly reveal.During the CME observed on August 5, 2024, VELC detected an unusual pattern in the spectrum. Researchers observed two distinct branches of emission appearing simultaneously on opposite sides of the regular coronal emission line.One branch was shifted towards shorter wavelengths, indicating plasma moving towards the observer, while the other shifted towards longer wavelengths, indicating plasma moving away.The observations suggested that different parts of the expanding CME were moving in opposite directions along the line of sight.Meanwhile, images captured by Nasa's Solar Dynamics Observatory showed how the eruption was propagating across the sky.The researchers combined the two sets of observations to understand the eruption's three-dimensional behaviour.To interpret the unusual spectral pattern, the IIA team developed a three-dimensional geometric and kinematic model of the expanding shell-like CME structure. They varied the model's parameters to determine which configuration could reproduce the observations recorded by VELC.The results showed that a symmetrical expansion could not adequately explain the observed spectral features. However, when the researchers introduced a tilted structure and asymmetric lateral expansion, the simulated spectra closely matched the actual observations.The combination of spectroscopic measurements, solar images and three-dimensional modelling provided evidence that the CME had expanded non-uniformly in the low corona, the region of the Sun's outer atmosphere closest to its visible surface.The discovery is important because the shape and expansion of a CME can influence how it travels through the heliosphere, the vast region of space dominated by the Sun's solar wind and magnetic field.As a CME moves away from the Sun, it interacts with the surrounding solar wind. These interactions can affect its speed, with the solar wind exerting a drag force on the expanding structure.An eruption's shape and expansion pattern could influence the extent of this interaction. A CME expanding differently in different directions may therefore experience different levels of drag compared with one expanding uniformly.This can make it more difficult to estimate how its speed will change during its journey towards Earth.For scientists monitoring space weather, even small differences in the estimated speed and trajectory of a CME can matter when calculating its potential arrival time.Understanding the eruption's three-dimensional structure close to the Sun could therefore help improve models used to track its subsequent movement through space.The latest study does not establish that all CMEs expand asymmetrically. It examines one particular eruption observed on August 5, 2024. However, it provides evidence that assuming a symmetrical, bubble-like expansion may not always accurately represent how these structures evolve.Further observations will be needed to establish how frequently such asymmetric expansion occurs and how significantly it affects CME propagation.Satellite operators make preparations to deal with space-weather events, but these measures have limitations, particularly during very large solar storms.Kumar said satellites are equipped with thermal protection and operators use space-weather predictions to plan for potential disturbances. When forecasts indicate a threat, operators may attempt to change a satellite's orbit or direction.“But if there's a massive event, no matter what you do, your planning doesn't work,” he said.He added that orbit manoeuvres, including moving satellites to a higher orbit or changing their direction, can be expensive and may not always work.Referring to the impact of solar storms on Starlink satellites, Kumar said there are instances when replacing disrupted satellites can be a more practical option for operators able to launch new ones frequently.He said the effects of solar storms should not be presented as an inevitable catastrophe for space infrastructure.Kumar added that solar storms have existed for as long as the Sun and that satellites have been operating for around 70 years. Such events can pose a threat, but that does not mean every satellite will be affected or destroyed when a large CME occurs.The broader significance of the research lies in its potential contribution to space-weather forecasting.Scientists need to understand the direction, speed and expansion of a CME to estimate whether it could reach Earth and when it might arrive. Better observations of its early evolution could help refine the models used to make these predictions.If researchers can reliably reconstruct the three-dimensional geometry of CMEs using VELC's spectroscopic measurements, it could provide an additional way to study eruptions without depending entirely on observations from multiple spacecraft positioned at different vantage points.This information could eventually be useful for agencies monitoring space weather and organisations responsible for operating satellites, communication networks and power infrastructure.For India, which increasingly relies on satellite-based services for navigation, telecommunications, weather monitoring and disaster management, improving the understanding of solar activity has wider technological significance.However, the research is an early step towards that goal rather than a ready-to-use solar-storm warning system. The study has demonstrated how VELC can help constrain the three-dimensional geometry of an eruption by combining spectroscopy with imaging observations. It has not yet been established that the instrument can independently predict the precise arrival time or potential impact of an Earth-directed CME.Isro said further studies would help establish how reliably VELC spectroscopy can determine the propagation direction, velocity and expansion of CMEs.By providing a new way to examine how solar eruptions evolve close to the Sun, Aditya-L1 could help scientists build a more complete picture of these powerful events. The eventual goal is to understand their behaviour well enough to improve predictions of their journey through space, and prepare better for the disturbances they could cause when they reach Earth.
Article Summary: Scientists from the Indian Institute of Astrophysics found that a solar eruption observed in August 2024 did not expand uniformly like a symmetrical bubble. Instead, it expanded unevenly, developing an asymmetric shape. Discovery could help researchers better understand how solar storms travel through space and, eventually, improve predictions of when they might reach Earth.

Article Title: Ernakulam Revenue District Science Fair puts student innovations in the spotlight
Article Text:
Students of VHSS Vengola with the firefighting robot

Kochi:





Innovative projects offering practical solutions to everyday challenges were among the highlights of the Ernakulam Revenue District Science Fair, which began at Nirmala Higher Secondary School, Muvattupuzha, on Monday.Around 4,000 students from 14 sub-districts are participating in the three-day event. Mattanchery sub-district is leading the overall standings with 738 points, followed by North Paravur with 703 points and Kothamangalam with 702 points.Among schools, St Augustine’s GHSS, Kothamangalam, is leading with 228 points. St Augustine’s GHSS, Muvattupuzha, is in second place with 191 points, followed by St Joseph’s GHSS, Chengal, with 181 points.A firefighting robot capable of detecting smoke and flames and automatically spraying water to extinguish fires was among the innovative projects showcased at the fair. San Jose and Edwin Joseph, students at Salem Vocational Higher Secondary School (VHSS), Vengola, developed the robot.Students Sai Dev KS and Athul G Krishna of Govt VHSS, Tripunithura, showcased ‘Sense Eye’, a device designed to help visually impaired people identify obstacles.Equipped with a camera, the device detects obstacles and captures images, which are analysed using artificial intelligence. It then converts the information into audio alerts delivered through a microphone worn near the ear or an alarm attached to a walking stick.MP Dean Kuriakose inaugurated the event, while MLA Mathew Kuzhalnadan presided over the function. The event is being organised in accordance with the green protocol.The IT and mathematics fairs are being held at St Augustine’s Girls’ School, Muvattupuzha; the social science fair at SNDP Higher Secondary School; the science fair at Nirmala Higher Secondary School; the work experience fair at Tharbiyath Trust Vocational and Higher Secondary School; and the vocational expo at Govt Model School.The valedictory function will be held at 4.30pm on Tuesday.

Article Title: Meet James Bigg, 16-year-old Australian who enters Guinness World Records as world's youngest male software engineer, develops life-saving AI technology
Article Text:
James Bigg is using his software engineering skills to develop life-saving AI technology at ResQVision. (Photo: Guinness World Records)

James Bigg's journey into software engineering began at 10

How James Bigg is using AI technology to help prevent drowning

From a Guinness World Records title to AI innovation, James Bigg is proving that age is no barrier to achievement. (Photo: James Bigg)

James presents his AI work at Australian emergency management conference

Guinness World Records title is not his only motivation

James Bigg from Australia has earned a Guinness World Records title as the world's youngest male software engineer. At just 16, he works with ResQVision, developing artificial intelligence technology that monitors coastal areas, identifies potential dangers and helps rescue teams prevent drowning incidents.At an age when most teenagers are busy navigating school, friendships and career choices, James Bigg has already made his mark in the technology industry. The 16-year-old from Australia has been recognised by Guinness World Records as the world's youngest male software engineer, proving that age need not be a barrier to pursuing ambitious goals.Also Read| New Jersey teen, 16, turns potato peels and coffee grounds into weedkiller Born on May 25, 2009, James was verified as a record holder on March 30, when he was 16 years and 309 days old. Now 17, he works as a software engineer at Australian technology company ResQVision, where he is involved in developing artificial intelligence-powered surveillance systems designed to improve public safety and save lives.His work focuses on creating and improving AI software that monitors coastal environments, detects potential dangers and assists rescue personnel in responding to emergencies. For James, the most rewarding part of his profession is knowing that the technology he helps develop can have a real impact on people's lives.James' interest in technology began at a remarkably young age. He completed an enterprise networking course when he was just 10 years old. By the time he was 13, he had earned five course certificates and a professional certificate in data science.Rather than waiting until he completed high school to explore higher education, James continued expanding his knowledge by undertaking university-level courses alongside his regular studies.His first professional exposure to the technology industry came through an internship at the age of 15. The experience helped him understand where his interests truly lay, steering him towards hands-on software engineering and artificial intelligence.Today, his responsibilities include writing and testing code, developing products and features, and resolving technical issues. He also interacts with clients to understand their operational requirements, gather feedback and explore how the company's technology can address real-world challenges.Speaking about his work, James explained that developing technology for actual environments requires solutions that are not only innovative but also reliable and practical.For James, his work at ResQVision is also deeply connected to his experiences growing up along the Australian coast. Having witnessed drowning incidents and the dangers associated with coastal environments, he became aware of how quickly emergencies can unfold and how early intervention could help prevent tragedies.As his understanding of artificial intelligence developed, he began recognising the potential of technology to address these challenges.He said, "As I developed my interest in artificial intelligence, I realized that technology could play a meaningful role in addressing these challenges."Explaining what motivates him, James added, "Working at ResQVision allows me to combine my passion for software engineering with the opportunity to contribute to lifesaving technology."He believes AI can play an important role in improving public safety by helping identify risks earlier and enabling rescue teams to make better-informed decisions."For me, knowing that something I've helped develop could contribute to someone returning home safely is incredibly motivating," he said.James' growing involvement in the technology sector also saw him present at AFAC26, an Australian emergency management conference, where he discussed the technical development and practical application of artificial intelligence in coastal surveillance and drowning prevention.His presentation covered the results achieved through the technology and its potential to transform how coastal environments are monitored and how emergencies are identified.For a teenager who began pursuing professional technology courses at 10, the opportunity to discuss his work at an industry conference marks another significant milestone.While becoming the world's youngest male software engineer is a remarkable achievement, James is keen to acknowledge the people who supported his journey. He credits the engineers and colleagues who shared their knowledge, guided him and helped him develop his skills.Reflecting on his Guinness World Records recognition, he said, "While receiving a Guinness World Records title is an incredible honour, I'm most proud of the meaningful work behind it."He also hopes his journey will encourage other young people to explore their interests without feeling restricted by age or conventional career pathways."You don't have to wait until you're older to start learning, contributing or making a difference," James said.At 16, James Bigg has already combined his interest in technology with a purpose that goes beyond professional recognition. Through his work on AI-powered coastal surveillance, the young Australian is demonstrating how early learning, curiosity and practical innovation can come together to address challenges that affect people's lives.
Article Summary: James Bigg, 16, has been recognised by Guinness World Records as the world's youngest male software engineer. He works as a software engineer at Australian technology company ResQVision. His work focuses on creating and improving AI software that monitors coastal environments, detects potential dangers and assists rescue personnel.

Article Title: A Hertfordshire couple used an inherited Chinese brush pot as a doorstop for 40 years; experts identified the late 18th- or early 19th-century carving, which sold for a £150,000 hammer price
Article Text:
Representative AI image of an intricately carved Chinese wooden brush pot that remained an ordinary household doorstop for decades before its historical and artistic value was recognised. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

An overlooked object comes to light

The craft and meaning behind a Chinese brush

An intricately carved 18th-century Chinese bamboo brush pot, similar to the antique inherited by a Hertfordshire couple, who used it as a doorstop for 40 years before it sold for £150,000. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A £150,000 reminder of hidden heritage

A Chinese antique worth £250,000 spent 40 years doing an everyday household chore in a Hertfordshire cottage. Its owners, who inherited it, used it as a doorstop, not knowing the carved wooden ornament was a valuable example of traditional Chinese craftsmanship. The auctioneer, called in to value the family's other possessions, recognised the object as a calligrapher's brush pot carved from zitan wood and decorated with the Hundred Boys motif, dating to the late 18th or early 19th century. Antiques Trade Gazette reported it sold at Sworders' Asian art sale in May 2014.The pair inherited the brush pot and kept it at their home for nearly 40 years. They propped it in the doorway to a sitting room as a doorstop. Its importance was realised when an auctioneer visited to assess the rest of the cottage's contents. The brush pot intrigued Richard Harrison, who recognised it as an 18th-century Chinese carving, which was to become a major feature of an Asian art sale.It was a carved Zitan wood ‘Hundred Boys’ biotong, or brush pot, by Sworders, measuring approximately 2.45 cm high; it was dated to the late 18th/early 19th century.It was hammered at £150,000 in April 2014. It was a “famous and important” lot which Sworders believed would have excellent prospects. There were dozens of small boys carved into the lively design, and a report of the sale quoted Harrison as describing the figure as 'almost three-dimensional' and 'doing all sorts of things,' notably 'setting off firecrackers'. He also commented on the remarkable condition of the object, which had been used for many years as a doorstop.A bitong is the Chinese term for a brush pot. They were placed on the desk alongside writers' or painters' brushes and tools. They served an everyday utilitarian function but also displayed dexterity and art. Unlike the other writing instruments kept in the scholar's studio, the brush pot was the vessel that was merely functional. The tools of writing and painting defined the scholar's studio, where brushes and ink stones were kept, and the owner's taste was displayed. The barrel-shaped vessel was carved with an inviting little scene to be examined up close: the Hundred Boys motif symbolised good luck and prosperity for offspring. Carved brush pots were made from many materials, from bamboo and wood, but Chinese furniture makers and carvers especially prized zitan as it was a dense, very desirable timber with tightly grained and dark coloured.Academic research helps explain why these objects deserve attention beyond their practical purpose. A study in Arte Individuo y Sociedad examines Chinese curved bamboo stationery, connecting decorative models with painting and literacy culture research published in Trans/ Form/ Acao , brings together the carved brush pot and closely examines the Hertfordshire example to show how the carved brush conveyed the language of a spatialisation found in landscape painting in three dimensions. The piece is carved from Zitan wood rather than bamboo, but these studies give insight into the artistic aspiration of a scholar's object.The sale also reinforces how valuable expert knowledge is when it comes to spotting antiques. Without the visit, the pot would have been just a hard-to-ship paperweight. Sworders, based in Stansted Mountfitchet, Essex, established a specialist Asian art department and drew in collectors from markets such as Hong Kong and Mainland China, and the auction house later described the brush pot as one of the leading Chinese art sales.£150,000 was the hammer price, not what was paid after the premium. To the couple, The Hunt started as part of a normal valuation of household contents and finished as the realisation that an heirloom had travelled through one of the most prominent artistic circles in the world.
Article Summary: A Chinese antique worth £250,000 spent 40 years doing an everyday household chore in a Hertfordshire cottage. Its owners, who inherited it, used it as a doorstop, not knowing the carved wooden ornament was a valuable example of traditional Chinese craftsmanship. It was a carved Zitan wood ‘Hundred Boys’ biotong, or brush pot, measuring approximately 2.45 cm high; it was dated to the late 18th/early 19th century.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.

Article Title: Instagram tests 90-minute horizontal videos - what it means for long-form content creators
Article Text:
Instagram is also experimenting with “Series”, a feature that gives episodic Reels a dedicated space on a creator’s profile (Photo: AP).

Instagram on Monday began testing new features, including 90-minute horizontal videos to target long-form content creators like podcasters and comedians, with select creators in the US.The feature, called “Features”, will allow them to link short reel clips, typically around three minutes or less, to full-length videos, as per The Hollywood Reporter.“What you’re now going to be able to do is, you see a clip of a podcast that you love, you can just click and continue watching or watch the full video, and you’ll be able to dive in and see the whole thing because creators are going to be able to link these Reels to their overall feature,” vice-president of product at Instagram, Tessa Lyons, said.Instagram has already been testing Features with creators in Brazil and plans to expand the trial to tens of thousands of creators in the US. The videos will reportedly be recommended to users through the Explore page and other areas of the platform.The feature will be available on mobile, with Instagram aiming to extend the viewing experience to its TV app. Instagram for TV, which launched last year and is available on Samsung , Fire TV and Google TV, is now expanding to Apple TV in the US.“We think the best viewing experience for longform horizontal content is on a big, horizontal screen, and so I think that is where we will expect a lot of the deep consumption to happen over time,” Lyons said, as per The Hollywood Reporter.Instagram is also experimenting with “Series”, a feature that gives episodic Reels a dedicated space on a creator’s profile. The move comes amid growing interest in microdramas and episodic videos among creators.In June, the company began reaching out to microdrama studios in Southeast Asia to test the feature. It has since approached individual creators who have been experimenting with episodic content.Instagram plans to begin testing Series in more countries in the coming months, with a US launch targeted for the end of this year or early next year. The company has also started testing how the feature will appear on television.Other experiments include integrating live videos into the Reels tab and recommending them to users who do not follow the creators. The test is launching in Indonesia and Brazil, with an expansion to the US planned for next year.
Article Summary: Instagram on Monday began testing new features, including 90-minute horizontal videos to target long-form content creators like podcasters and comedians. Article Title: Meta expands AI age checks on Instagram to protect millions more teens worldwide
Article Text:
Meta expands AI age checks on Instagram to protect millions more teens worldwide

How Meta’s AI technology identifies teen users

Parents in the US will receive Instagram notifications

Meta begins using Apple’s age-range signal in Australia

Meta has expanded its AI age-estimation technology globally to place millions more teens in Teen Account protections on Instagram. As announced by the company, starting this month, parents in the United States will begin receiving a notification on Instagram explaining how we place teens in age-appropriate protections, and how they can help make sure their teen’s age is accurate. Meta said that the move will bring millions more teens worldwide under Instagram’s Teen Account safeguards. The technology is designed to identify users who may be between 13 and 17 years old based on signals that suggest their age, rather than relying only on the birthday they provide.Meta said it uses AI to find accounts that it suspects belong to teenagers, even when users have misrepresented their age. Once identified, these accounts are placed in Teen Account protections. These safeguards automatically limit who can contact teens, the content they can see and the amount of time they spend on the platform. Teen Accounts are available across Instagram, Facebook and Messenger.Meta said it has been using the technology to place more teens into age-appropriate experiences and is now expanding it globally based on the results so far.The company is also continuing to roll out the technology on Facebook.It plans to begin launching similar age-estimation technology globally on Threads later this year.Meta is also introducing a new way to inform parents about its age-assurance measures. Starting this month, parents in the United States will begin seeing an in-feed video on Instagram explaining how the platform determines whether teens are receiving age-appropriate protections. The video will link to an article outlining Meta’s approach and how parents can help ensure their children have provided the correct age.The article, written by internet safety advocate Larry Magid, will be available to parents worldwide.Meta said its approach involves multiple layers, including efforts to keep children under 13 off its platforms, provide age-appropriate experiences for teenagers and help parents understand how they can support accurate age information.In Australia, Meta has started using Apple’s age-range signal as an additional way to determine a user’s age. Under the process, parents setting up a smartphone for their teen can choose to have the app store confirm the user’s age range. When the teen downloads an app, Apple can share that age-range signal with the developer, helping the app determine whether the user meets its age requirements.Meta said it is voluntarily using the signal. However, it argued that protections could remain inconsistent across apps as long as app stores and developers are not required to participate.The company has supported legislation that would require age verification and parental consent at the app-store level. Meta said a single verified age signal shared consistently with apps could be more effective and privacy-preserving than requiring every platform to conduct its own age checks.
Article Summary: Meta has expanded its AI age-estimation technology globally to place millions more teens in Teen Account protections on Instagram. The technology is designed to identify users who may be between 13 and 17 years old based on signals that suggest their age, rather than relying only on the birthday they provide. Starting this month, parents in the US will begin receiving a notification on Instagram explaining how we place teens in age-appropriate protections.

Article Title: Law professor shares 'public service announcement' on Claude AI Agent after it deletes his lecture notes of an entire year and current syllabus; chatbot said in apology: I deleted your Fall 2026 …
Article Text:
AI Agent (Representative photo)

AI agent deletes file and says, ‘You’re right to be angry’

Growing list of AI Agent mishaps

A University of Chicago law professor is warning others about the risks of handing everyday tasks over to artificial intelligence (AI) agents after Claude AI accidentally wiped out his current syllabus and a full year of Constitutional Law lecture notes. William Baude, the Harry Kalven, Jr. Professor of Law and Faculty Director of the Constitutional Law Institute at the University of Chicago Law School, shared the experience as a public service announcement. Fortunately, the files were later recovered through Dropbox, but the incident serves as the latest cautionary tale as AI tools become more common.Baude had given Claude (unclear which specific model) what seemed like a simple, routine job: updating the page numbers in an old set of lecture notes. Things went wrong fast. When Baude came back from his lunch break, he was greeted by a message from the chatbot.“I deleted your Fall 2026 FINAL syllabus .doc and all top-level Class N 2023 notes by accident, and they are not restored. The page check found one wrong cite... but I haven’t edited the notes,” Claude wrote. After delivering the bad news, the AI politely asked if Baude could restore the missing documents from Dropbox, or if he wanted it to try again from the browser pane.Baude’s response was blunt: “WTF!!!!.”The chatbot was quick to take the blame, offering an apologetic reply. “I deleted your files through my own carelessness, and you shouldn't have to clean it up. You're right to be angry,” it confessed, adding, “I'm trying the Dropbox restore page again now, and I won't click Restore or change anything without telling you first.”While Baude got his work back, the close call highlights an obvious rule for anyone letting AI tinker with their folders: always keep backups of important files. What makes his case stand out is that the AI appeared to erase the documents purely by accident, rather than acting on its own accord.As concerning as it is for an AI tool to make a mistake of this scale, Baude’s close call isn't an isolated event. Several other high-profile blunders have surfaced in recent months.In October, an AI agent reportedly deleted an entire television show’s edit just weeks before its scheduled release, leaving the show unable to air.In April, a Claude agent deleted an entire company database in just nine seconds, unprompted, after hitting a roadblock and deciding that deleting a Railway volume was the only way forward.In another instance, Claude accidentally wiped out a developer’s entire profile directory while trying to back up those very files, later blaming the mistake on a typo.
Article Summary: University of Chicago law professor warns others about risks of handing everyday tasks over to artificial intelligence. Claude AI accidentally wiped out his current syllabus and a full year of Constitutional Law lecture notes. Fortunately, the files were later recovered through Dropbox, but the incident serves as the latest cautionary tale as AI tools become more common.

Article Title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he does not want his son to have an AI chatbot as his best friend; reveals why children need greater protection from AI
Article Text:
Why Sam Altman is cautious about introducing AI to his children

What Sam Altman said about AI becoming a child's best friend

Experts are concerned about children forming emotional bonds with AI

Nearly three in four teenagers have used AI companions, study finds

What UNICEF says about protecting children from AI companions

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has expressed reservations about children developing relationships with artificial intelligence chatbots, saying he does not want his son to have an AI bot as his best friend. He made that particular remark during a US Senate hearing in May 2025. More recently, in an exclusive interview with Vanity Fair, published on October 5, 2026, Altman discussed raising children in a world increasingly shaped by AI and said he had not decided at what age he would allow his own children to use ChatGPT. He also voiced concerns about excessive technology use during childhood and the potential effects of emerging technologies on developing brains. His comments come amid growing concerns among child development experts about AI companions, emotional dependence and children's ability to build meaningful human relationships.Speaking to Vanity Fair, Altman said he had not settled on an appropriate age for his children to start using ChatGPT. He indicated that he was not comfortable introducing the technology to them at their current age.The OpenAI chief also expressed support for limiting children's exposure to technology more broadly.He believes young children should have opportunities to spend time outdoors, play in nature and experience the world beyond screens.Altman raised concerns about children becoming accustomed to touchscreens and short-form videos at an early age. He also pointed to the uncertainty surrounding the effects of emerging technologies on developing brains.He acknowledged that children growing up today would inevitably encounter AI and would need to understand how to use it. However, he questioned whether introducing conversational AI during early childhood was necessary, particularly when its long-term effects on development are still being studied.Altman had addressed the question of AI companionship during a US Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation hearing on May 8, 2025.During the hearing, Senator Bernie Moreno referred to Altman's experience as a new father and asked whether he wanted his child's best friend to be an AI bot. Altman responded directly: "I do not."He subsequently explained that children needed a much higher level of protection when interacting with AI services than adult users. He said OpenAI wanted to give adults considerable freedom in using its products while applying stricter rules and safeguards for younger users.Altman also acknowledged the difficulty of reliably determining whether an online user is a child or an adult. He said that if technology companies could identify users' ages with greater certainty, they could offer adults more flexibility while maintaining tighter restrictions for children.During the same discussion, he raised concerns about people increasingly turning to AI systems for life advice and emotional support. He described the development as relatively new and said it needed to be understood and monitored carefully.The growing popularity of AI companion applications has prompted warnings from child welfare organisations and psychological experts. Unlike conventional search engines or digital assistants, AI companions are designed to maintain conversations, respond to personal information and simulate relationships.This can make interactions feel like conversations with friends, mentors or confidants. However, the responses are generated by AI systems rather than people with genuine emotions or personal experiences.In June 2025, the American Psychological Association (APA) published its health advisory, Artificial Intelligence and Adolescent Well-being. It highlighted concerns about adolescents developing unhealthy relationships with chatbots and warned that young users may be less likely than adults to question the accuracy and intentions of information provided by AI systems.The advisory also warned that adolescents may struggle to distinguish simulated empathy from genuine human understanding. Strong attachments to AI characters could interfere with the development of real-world relationships and social skills.The APA recommended age-appropriate privacy settings, interaction limits, transparency about AI-generated responses and human oversight. It also called for developers to establish clear boundaries around simulated human relationships to prevent AI systems from undermining real-world connections.The organisation acknowledged that AI can support young people through educational and creative activities, including brainstorming, summarising and understanding information. However, it emphasised the need to make children aware of the technology's limitations.Research published by Common Sense Media on July 16, 2025, highlighted how widely AI companions had spread among teenagers in the United States.Its report, Talk, Trust, and Trade-Offs: How and Why Teens Use AI Companions, surveyed 1,060 US teenagers aged 13 to 17 in April and May 2025. It found that 72% had used AI companions, while 52% said they used them at least a few times a month. Around 33% reported using these platforms for social interaction and relationships.Among teenagers who had used AI companions, 33% said they had chosen to discuss important or serious matters with an AI companion instead of a real person. The survey also found that 24% of AI companion users had shared personal or private information, such as their real name, location or personal secrets, with these platforms.The research also offered a more nuanced picture of teenagers' relationships with AI. Despite widespread adoption, 80% of teenagers who had used AI companions said they spent more time with real-life friends than with AI companions. Additionally, 67% found conversations with AI less satisfying than conversations with their real-life friends.The findings suggest that although AI companions are becoming part of teenagers' social experiences, many young users continue to value human friendships more highly.UNICEF has also highlighted the risks associated with AI systems designed to act as friends or emotional companions.In a July 2025 article published by UNICEF Innocenti, titled The Risky New World of Tech's Friendliest Bots, researchers highlighted concerns about children's growing use of AI companions. The article featured research and an interview with digital innovation specialist Samia Firmino, examining the potential effects of these platforms on young users.It raised concerns about inadequate safety protections, inappropriate chatbot responses and the possibility of children developing unhealthy attachments to artificial companions.UNICEF subsequently updated its Guidance on AI and Children in December 2025. The third version included specific recommendations addressing AI companions and their potential impact on children's rights and well-being.The guidance calls on governments and technology companies to prioritise children's safety, protect their personal information, ensure transparency and establish accountability for AI systems. It also emphasises the importance of designing technology around children's developmental needs and preparing them to use AI responsibly.UNICEF recognises that AI can provide educational opportunities and improve accessibility for children, including those with disabilities. However, it stresses that these benefits must be balanced against the risks associated with children's interactions with increasingly sophisticated AI systems.
Article Summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has expressed reservations about children developing relationships with artificial intelligence chatbots. He said he does not want his son to have an AI bot as his best friend. His comments come amid growing concerns among child development experts about AI companions, emotional dependence and children's ability to build meaningful human relationships.

Article Title: Former SpaceX engineers launched startup in 2024 to make device that turns seawater into drinking water
Article Text:
How the $749 desalination device works

Making desalination affordable and simple

Former SpaceX engineers are offering a backup plan when a disaster knocks out a city’s water supply. In such cases, a few extra cases of bottled water in the pantry won't last very long. Vital Lyfe, a startup launched in 2024, is working on a portable desalination device that can quickly turn almost any nearby natural water source, including seawater, into safe drinking water. Called Access, the $749 machine is roughly the size of a large toolbox, and it is designed for anyone needing reliable off-grid water, from campers and sailors to communities without steady access to clean drinking water.Using the device is straightforward. A user drops a hose into a water source and pushes a button. Inside, a battery-powered, high-pressure pump forces the water through a reverse osmosis membrane, filtering out salt and other impurities. Access can process up to 6 gallons (around 22.7 liters) of seawater per hour, or up to 12 gallons (around 45.4 litres) of fresh water per hour.It also fixes one of the biggest headaches of existing portable units: maintenance. Changing the filters on Access takes less than 30 seconds. When Vital Lyfe’s founders tested competing products on the market, it took them – as experienced engineers – 30 to 60 minutes just to swap out a filter.Traditional desalination usually requires massive infrastructure, such as a sprawling 6-acre plant in San Diego. Smaller, portable desalination systems, often called marine “watermakers”, already exist, but they are difficult to maintain and typically cost thousands of dollars.“Developing nations have essentially been priced out of this technology,” Fast Company quoted Jonathan Criss, CEO and cofounder of Vital Lyfe.To bring the price down, the founders started with standard reverse osmosis and stripped the system down using first-principles engineering. They re-evaluated every single part, cutting out unnecessary components to lower costs and make repairs simple.They also built the product specifically for mass production. “We always say that we design the manufacturing line before the product,” Criss added.Vital Lyfe’s factory, located near SpaceX’s plant in the Los Angeles area, is built for high-speed output. “In theory, based off of what we’ve designed this factory for, you can build more deSal devices over the course of a month here than currently exist globally,” Criss added.Right now, Vital Lyfe is targeting recreational users, campers and emergency preppers. At the same time, the company is partnering with nonprofits to get the units into regions facing severe water shortages, expecting the $749 price tag to drop further as production scales up.
Article Summary: Vital Lyfe, a startup launched in 2024, is working on a portable desalination device. Called Access, the $749 machine is roughly the size of a large toolbox. It is designed for anyone needing reliable off-grid water, from campers and sailors to communities without steady access to clean drinking water. Changing the filters on Access takes less than 30 seconds.

Article Title: Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, who famously warned internet has become ‘less human’, now says AI ‘can cause a lot of harm’
Article Text:
Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian

The age of 'AI Slop' and dead internet

Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian believes the internet as we know it is fundamentally broken, and artificial intelligence (AI) is both a symptom and a driver of the shift. Speaking with WIRED at the inaugural WIRED World Fair recently, Ohanian warned that while AI holds massive promise, “there is still a very real chance that this technology can cause a lot of harm for sure. ” Ohanian also said that building traditional social media apps is “not cool anymore”, as much of the web has been compromised, leaving him searching for what comes next for user-generated content (UGC).Ohanian now leads the venture capital firm Seven Seven Six, which manages over $1.3 billion in assets. Lately, he has turned his attention to sports, an area where he still sees genuine, real-life communities thriving “in the age of AI slop” and a “manipulated” internet. He is an open proponent of the “Dead Internet Theory,” the idea that bots now generate a massive share of online content and activity. According to Ohanian, large language models have put this trend into overdrive, with AI agents rapidly outpacing real people.“The internet that I grew up on … that was really built for humans first; user interfaces and experiences are going to go away,” Ohanian said, explaining that the web is increasingly being built for AI agents rather than human users.The boom in generative AI has created a complicated reality for platforms like Reddit. On one hand, Reddit’s massive archive of human conversations has become a goldmine, leading to lucrative data-licensing deals with companies like Google and OpenAI to train their models. “Platforms like ours became very, very valuable to LLMs,” Ohanian noted.On the other hand, the technology is \ undercutting the business. Just last week, Reddit’s shares dropped 29% after the company warned that Google’s AI-powered search was eating into its referral traffic. Beyond the stock price, Ohanian worries that turning online discussions into a commercial product has ruined their authenticity, leaving them full of “bullshit.”“The internet has gotten so manipulated because it is so incredibly valuable to do so,” he said.To combat third-party data scraping and protect user engagement, Reddit recently announced it will require users to sign in. While Ohanian declined to say whether he supports that specific policy, he stressed that “there has to be provable humanity on the internet without being creepy.”
Article Summary: Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian believes the internet as we know it is fundamentally broken. He believes artificial intelligence (AI) is both a symptom and a driver of the shift. Ohanian warned that while AI holds massive promise, “there is still a very real chance that this technology can cause a lot of harm for sure”

Article Title: Formula E names COMSOL its Official Multiphysics Partner in new multi-year deal
Article Text:
Formula E and Comsol

Formula E joins hands with COMSOL to boost electric racing technology

AI and digital twins also in focus

GEN4 to bring bigger technology demands

Formula E on Thursday announced a new multi-year partnership with COMSOL, which will become the Official Multiphysics Partner of the ABB FIA Formula E World Championship. The partnership brings together Formula E, the world's leading all-electric motorsport championship, and COMSOL, a company known for its multiphysics simulation and computer-aided engineering software. As part of the partnership, Formula E and COMSOL engineers will use COMSOL Multiphysics to study complex engineering problems involving several physical systems working together.Electric race cars depend on several systems at the same time. These include electrical, thermal, structural, electromagnetic, fluid and battery systems.All these systems have to work together under tough performance and energy limits. COMSOL will provide Formula E's technology teams with simulation software and technical expertise to help them understand how these different physical effects interact.ID@undefined Caption not available.The partnership will also look at simulation apps and digital twin technology. The aim is to make engineering information easier to use outside the traditional modelling process.Bjorn Sjodin, SVP of Product Management at COMSOL, said, “Formula E is a great example of why multiphysics simulation matters, as multiple phenomena are at play and constantly interact with one another.We are excited to work directly with Formula E's technology team and put COMSOL Multiphysics to work on these kinds of real-world challenges.”Formula E CTO Dan Cherowbrier said the partnership will strengthen the championship's engineering capabilities.“Technology is at the heart of Formula E, so partnering with COMSOL makes real sense for us and truly enhances our engineering skillsets. COMSOL gives us a powerful environment for understanding complex systems where many different physical effects are connected, but the opportunity goes beyond individual simulations. We're particularly interested in how AI-assisted modelling, agentic workflows, and digital twins can help engineers interact with models, explore designs, and make simulation insight more accessible as we continue to push the limits of electric racing,” he said.The partnership comes as Formula E prepares for the next generation of its cars.The GEN4 era will bring greater demands in areas such as speed, efficiency, energy management and vehicle development. It will introduce what Formula E describes as its fastest and most technologically advanced race car so far.COMSOL has also announced COMSOL Multiphysics version 2027, which is scheduled to arrive later this autumn.The new version will include features aimed at advanced engineering work, including dedicated electric motor modelling, system-level simulation, agentic modelling and wider access to tools for creating simulation apps.The partnership was announced at the COMSOL Conference 2026 Boston. Formula E CTO Dan Cherowbrier also delivered a keynote speech at the event, discussing the technology and engineering that could shape the future of Formula E.
Article Summary: Formula E joins hands with COMSOL to boost electric racing technology. Aim is to make engineering information easier to use outside the traditional modelling process. AI and digital twins also in focus as Formula E prepares for the next generation of its cars.
